newsitem.title: UK: Redwood hits campaign trail -- for UK Major's job.
newsitem.headline: Redwood hits campaign trail -- for UK Major's job.

text.p: Nearly two years after he tried to unseat John Major as Conservative party leader, John Redwood is still running hard for the top job.
One of the sub-plots to the general election campaign under way in Britain is who would replace Major if he lost the May 1 contest, which polls say is likely, and were then to quit.
While other leading members of the ruling party pledge undying loyalty to the prime minister, Redwood frankly acknowledges that the flame of ambition still burns bright.
"If he resigns and creates a vacancy, of course I will fight it," Redwood, whose cold intellectualism earned him the nickname Vulcan after the Star Trek character Mr Spock, told Reuters.
When Major challenged his detractors in June 1995 to "put up or shut up" and fight him for the job, Redwood quit the cabinet to pick up the gauntlet for the Conservative right wing.
"No change, no chance," he said then of the party's chances of a fifth straight term of office if Major stayed at the helm.

Decency prevents him from repeating the slogan now in the heat of battle, but he is still rattling Major's cage by openly defying the party line that Britain should keep its options open whether to join Europe's planned single currency.
Conservative strategists are praying that Europe, which has deeply divided the party, will not be a big election issue.
So Major's aides reacted with dismay when Redwood announced he was pushing ahead with the publication this week of a book arguing in the strongest terms against the single currency.
"Our Currency, Our Country" will be launched at a signing session on Wednesday, all but ensuring the media will once again pick at the scabs covering the party's wounds on Europe.

In what opposition politicians at least saw as an equally provocative move, Redwood went ahead on Tuesday with a trip to Wolverhampton, an industrial town in central England, after he learnt that Major was due to campaign just a few miles away.

Estelle Morris, a local Labour member of parliament (MP), declared the twin visits to be the "opening rounds in the battle for the leadership party... Today's shambles is the clearest proof yet of the civil war that has engulfed the Tories."

"The idea that the press has that the Tory party is completely divided on the issue is hogwash," Redwood, flanked by fellow Conservative Euro-sceptic Nicholas Budgen, the local MP whose vote he would need in a leadership fight, told reporters.
Skipping over the single currency split, Redwood deftly argued that Conservatives saw eye to eye on the big issue.

"I've spoken to dozens and dozens of Conservative associations around the country over the last year or so. We are united as one in the party in the country in wanting a common market, but not more common government," he said.

During his assiduous courting of Conservative activists on the rubber-chicken dinner circuit, Redwood said he had concentrated just as much on the need to reform the welfare state and cut taxes as he had on Europe.

But it was letters on Europe that filled his postbag, and whether the Conservative high command liked it or not, Europe was bound to be an election issue because of the profound impact that Brussels has on Britain's economic and social policy.
"So of course we're all going to be discussing it," Redwood said. Major, travelling back to London, had been warned.
